chunks: My father (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, saying: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr al-Bazanty, from Abdullah ibn Sin'an, from Al-Walid ibn Sabih, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I was with him, and there was a tray of fresh dates with him. A beggar came and he gave him (some dates). Then another beggar came and he gave him. Then another came and he gave him. Then another came, and he said to him: 'May God grant you an increase of sustenance!'

Then he said: 'If a man had wealth amounting to thirty or forty thousand (dinars), and he wished that nothing of it remain except that he distribute it in charity, he would do so, but he would be left with no wealth, and thus become one of the three whose prayers are returned to themselves.'

I said: 'May I be your ransom! Who are they?' He said: 'A man to whom God, the Exalted, granted wealth, so he spent it in its various forms, then he said: O Lord, grant me sustenance! [And God, the Exalted, says to him: Did I not grant you sustenance?]
And a man who curses his wife while he is being oppressive to her, and it is said to him: 'Did I not entrust her affairs to your care?'

And a man who sits in his house and abandons seeking (livelihood), then he says: O Lord, grant me sustenance! [God] the Exalted says to him: 'Did I not establish for you the means to seek sustenance?'

key_terms.وَسَعَهُ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكَ: May God grant you an increase of sustenance

ai.seo_question: Who are the three people whose prayers for sustenance are not answered?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Khisal*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the theological principle that divine sustenance is linked to human effort and gratitude, identifying three specific categories whose supplications are rejected due to negligence or injustice. The first group squanders their wealth to the point of destitution before asking for more, the second oppresses their wives while demanding relief, and the third remains idle, failing to utilize the means of provision God has made accessible. This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the balance between reliance on God (Tawakkul) and active striving (Tadbeer) in acquiring sustenance.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 3-208 (The compiler of the book narrated) that his father - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Sa’ed ibn Abdullah quoted on the authority of Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, on the authority of Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr al-Bazanty, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Sin’an, on the authority of Al-Walid ibn Sabih who said,

“I was with Aba Abdullah as-Sadiq (MGB). A tray of dates was in front of him (MGB). A beggar came and the Imam (MGB) gave him some dates. Another one came and the Imam (MGB) gave him some dates. A third beggar came, but the Imam (MGB) said, ‘May God grant you an increase of sustenance!’

Then the Imam (MGB) told me, ‘If a man has more than thirty or forty-thousand (Dinars) and wishes to give it all away in charity, he can do so, but he will become poor and will be amongst those whose prayers are returned to themselves.’

I asked the Imam (MGB), ‘May I be your ransom! Who are these people?’ The Imam (MGB) replied, ‘They include men to whom God has granted what they prayed for, but spend it all for God’s sake and again say, ‘O God! Please give me more sustenance!’
They also include men who curse their wives while having treated their wives oppressively. They are told, ‘Have We not entrusted her affairs with you?’

They also include men who sit in their house, pray to seek their sustenance and say, ‘O God! Please deliver my sustenance to me! The Honorable the Exalted God tells them, ‘Have I not established a way for you to obtain your daily sustenance?’”
